1	# Etymology verification task — instructions
2	
3	You are verifying the etymological derivations from Ali Nourai's *An Etymological
4	Dictionary of Persian, English and other Indo-European Languages* (1999), which this
5	repository (`/home/sfmqrb/git/rishe`) turned into JSON (`data/extracted/batch/page-<pdf>.json`).
6	Compact text renderings of the charts are in
7	`/home/sfmqrb/git/rishe/data/verification/agent/charts/page-<pdf>.txt`.
8	
9	Each chart is a tree: a ROOT box, then nodes `#id (parent #p) [Language] refs=… | word «script» : gloss`.
10	An arrow parent→child in the book means "child derives from parent". `parent #0` = derives from the root.
11	Redirect entries (`ROOT X -> redirect to Y`) need no verification: skip them (do not include them).
12	
13	## Your job, per chart (entry)
14	
15	1. Verify the ROOT itself: is the reconstructed root real, is the language label right,
16	   is the gloss right? (e.g. PIE *dʰeyǵʰ- "knead, form" — Pokorny 244.)
17	2. Verify EVERY node (every derivation edge parent→child, and every word in the node):
18	   - Is the word real, in that language, with that meaning?
19	   - Does it really descend from (or was borrowed from) the parent as drawn?
20	   - Give the **derivation explanation**: how, phonetically and historically, the child form
21	     arises from the parent form. Be concrete: name the sound changes (e.g. "Av. pairi-daēza-
22	     → MP *pardēz; Greek borrowed it in the 5th c. BCE as paradeisos (Xenophon), Greek
23	     -ei- rendering Iranian -ē-; Latin paradīsus; Old French paradis; Middle English
24	     paradis > paradise"), the route of borrowing (which people/era/text), and the
25	     semantic shift ("walled enclosure" → "royal park" → "Garden of Eden" via the Septuagint).
26	     For Persian words descend through Old Iranian → Middle Persian → New Persian and name
27	     the intermediate forms when sources give them (e.g. OP didā- / Av. daēza- → MP diz →
28	     NP dež/dez). For Arabic loans note the Arabic stem, and for Arabic-mediated round-trips
29	     (Persian → Arabic → Persian) say so.
30	3. Give a verdict per node and per root:
31	   - `confirmed` — independent modern sources agree with the chart (same root, same route).
32	   - `plausible` — sources give a compatible but not identical picture, or the derivation
33	     is accepted by some scholars but not all; explain the difference.
34	   - `disputed` — modern scholarship (Wiktionary with citations, Etymonline, AHD, Cheung,
35	     Hasandust, Beekes, de Vaan, Kroonen, MacKenzie…) prefers a DIFFERENT origin, or the
36	     word is unrelated. Explain what the modern view is.
37	   - `unverified` — you could not find any independent source either way (say what you tried).
38	   - `transcription_suspect` — the form in the JSON is not what the sources know (a misread
39	     letter, an impossible form, a wrong Persian script). See "Transcription flags" below:
40	     you must check the printed page and say whether the book or the extraction is at fault.
41	4. Record sources as URLs (Wiktionary page, Etymonline page, AHD appendix entry, archive.org
42	   page of Klein/Horn/Bartholomae, etc.). Also note when Nourai's own cited reference

# Etymology verification task — instructions

You are verifying the etymological derivations from Ali Nourai's *An Etymological
Dictionary of Persian, English and other Indo-European Languages* (1999), which this
repository (`/home/sfmqrb/git/rishe`) turned into JSON (`data/extracted/batch/page-<pdf>.json`).
Compact text renderings of the charts are in
`/home/sfmqrb/git/rishe/data/verification/agent/charts/page-<pdf>.txt`.

Each chart is a tree: a ROOT box, then nodes `#id (parent #p) [Language] refs=… | word «script» : gloss`.
An arrow parent→child in the book means "child derives from parent". `parent #0` = derives from the root.
Redirect entries (`ROOT X -> redirect to Y`) need no verification: skip them (do not include them).

## Your job, per chart (entry)

1. Verify the ROOT itself: is the reconstructed root real, is the language label right,
   is the gloss right? (e.g. PIE *dʰeyǵʰ- "knead, form" — Pokorny 244.)
2. Verify EVERY node (every derivation edge parent→child, and every word in the node):
   - Is the word real, in that language, with that meaning?
   - Does it really descend from (or was borrowed from) the parent as drawn?
   - Give the **derivation explanation**: how, phonetically and historically, the child form
     arises from the parent form. Be concrete: name the sound changes (e.g. "Av. pairi-daēza-
     → MP *pardēz; Greek borrowed it in the 5th c. BCE as paradeisos (Xenophon), Greek
     -ei- rendering Iranian -ē-; Latin paradīsus; Old French paradis; Middle English
     paradis > paradise"), the route of borrowing (which people/era/text), and the
     semantic shift ("walled enclosure" → "royal park" → "Garden of Eden" via the Septuagint).
     For Persian words descend through Old Iranian → Middle Persian → New Persian and name
     the intermediate forms when sources give them (e.g. OP didā- / Av. daēza- → MP diz →
     NP dež/dez). For Arabic loans note the Arabic stem, and for Arabic-mediated round-trips
     (Persian → Arabic → Persian) say so.
3. Give a verdict per node and per root:
   - `confirmed` — independent modern sources agree with the chart (same root, same route).
   - `plausible` — sources give a compatible but not identical picture, or the derivation
     is accepted by some scholars but not all; explain the difference.
   - `disputed` — modern scholarship (Wiktionary with citations, Etymonline, AHD, Cheung,
     Hasandust, Beekes, de Vaan, Kroonen, MacKenzie…) prefers a DIFFERENT origin, or the
     word is unrelated. Explain what the modern view is.
   - `unverified` — you could not find any independent source either way (say what you tried).
   - `transcription_suspect` — the form in the JSON is not what the sources know (a misread
     letter, an impossible form, a wrong Persian script). See "Transcription flags" below:
     you must check the printed page and say whether the book or the extraction is at fault.
4. Record sources as URLs (Wiktionary page, Etymonline page, AHD appendix entry, archive.org
   page of Klein/Horn/Bartholomae, etc.). Also note when Nourai's own cited reference

- **Scanned references without full OCR text** (Borhan-e Qate' vols 3–5 = BQT pages

other books in the local library that could speak to that claim, and record what each says.

`/home/sfmqrb/git/rishe/data/verification/sources/SOURCE_MATRIX.md`. Minimum per node:

- an Indo-European node or root box: Pokorny (POK) AND Walde-Pokorny (WLD) AND Watkins/AHD,
  plus Mann (IEC) or Buck (SYN) when the word is a common noun;
- an Avestan / Old Persian node: Bartholomae (BRT) or Kent (KNT);
- a Pahlavi / Middle Persian node: MacKenzie (PHD) and Nyberg (NYB);
- a New Persian node: Horn (HRN), Hübschmann (HUB), Cheung (CHEUNG, for verbs), Borhan-e
  Qate' with Mo'in's footnotes (BQT), Mo'in (MON), and Aryanpur (ARY);
- a Sogdian node: Gharib (SOD); a Khotanese one: Bailey (ISS_alt_DKS);
- an Arabic node or a Persian/Arabic loan in either direction: Klein (KLN), Jeffery (FVQ),
  Addi Shir (AFM), Asbaghi (PLA), Fraenkel (AFA), Lokotsch (LKT); for French/Spanish
  Arabisms Pihan (PHN), Devic (DEV), Lammens (LAM), Dozy (DOZ);
- an English / Romance node: Klein (KLN), Skeat (SKT), Funk & Wagnalls (FSD), Webster (WEB);
  Anglo-Indian words: Hobson-Jobson (HJB), Whitworth (AID);
- a Turkic node: Vámbéry (TTS), Lokotsch (LKT).

Grep each file for the headword (several spellings; Latin transliteration for the Western
books, Persian script for BQT/MON/ARY, Pahlavi transliteration for PHD/NYB). A grep that
finds nothing is also a result ("silent"). Record everything in a `consulted` array on the
node (separate from `ref_check`, which is only for the references Nourai himself cites):

```json

  {"src": "HRN", "where": "no. 3, p. 1", "stance": "contradicts", "note": "Horn separates āb 'Glanz' from āb 'water' and derives āftāb from the former"},
  {"src": "PHD", "where": "p. 5 s.v. ābād", "stance": "supports", "note": "'ābād [ʾpʾt] populous, thriving' — no water element"},
  {"src": "WLD", "where": "Bd. I p. 46", "stance": "silent", "note": "root ap- listed, no Persian compound"}
]
```

`stance` ∈ supports / contradicts / partial / silent. Quote the key phrase. Books consulted
via the web (vajehyab for Mo'in, AHD online) go here too, with the URL archived via
fetch_source.py and listed in `sources`. Every node must have at least two `consulted`
entries from different books whenever the matrix lists two or more books for its language.

For every node you mark `transcription_suspect`, look at the printed page itself — render it
with `pdftoppm -f <pdf page> -l <pdf page> -r 300 -png -singlefile /home/sfmqrb/git/rishe/EtymologicalDictionary-persian-english.pdf /tmp/pg<pdf page>`
(or open `site/pages/<pdf page>.jpg`) and Read the image — and add to the node:

```json
"error_in": "book",            // "book" = the printed book has the odd form (author's misprint); the extraction is faithful
                               // "extraction" = the book prints the correct form; the JSON misread it
                               // "unknown" = could not decide from the image
"book_prints": "borrāgō",      // what the printed page actually shows
"correct_form": "borrāgō"      // the form that should stand (per the sources)
```

Usually the extraction is faithful and the problem is in the book itself; say so plainly in
`derivation` too ("the book prints X; this is Nourai's misprint for Y"). Only when the JSON
differs from the page is it an extraction error (report those separately in your summary — the
owner fixes the data). Copy the page PNG you relied on to
`data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/<pdf page>.png` so the check can be audited.

## Persian explanation (required): `derivation_fa` on every node, `note_fa` on every root

Write the derivation a second time IN PERSIAN, for a Persian reader — not a translation of the
English sentence. Think about how a Persian etymologist (حسن‌دوست، ابوالقاسمی، معین در حواشی
برهان قاطع) would explain it to an educated Persian reader:

- Use the established Persian terminology: هندواروپایی آغازین، ایرانی باستان، اوستایی، پارسی
  باستان، فارسی میانه (پهلوی)، پارتی، سغدی، فارسی نو/دری؛ وام‌واژه، وام‌گیری، دگرگونی آوایی،
  قلب (metathesis)، ابدال، همگونی، پیشوند، پسوند، ریشه، ستاک، تحول معنایی، معرّب، ریشه‌شناسی
  عامیانه (folk etymology)، هم‌ریشه (cognate)، دوگانه (doublet).

  as Persian philology does (e.g. «آب» از فارسی میانهٔ āb / āp، از ایرانی باستان *āp-، هم‌ریشه با
  سنسکریت āp-). Persian-script forms for Arabic words; Greek/Latin words in Latin letters.

  دو واکه در فارسی میانه به ب نرم شده»؛ «ای کشیدهٔ فارسی میانه در فارسی نو به ی بدل شده»).

# Source matrix — which local books to grep for each kind of node

All files are OCR text; pages are separated by form-feeds (`\f`) and, in the `_pages.txt` files, tagged `[pdf page N]`. Print one page with `awk 'BEGIN{RS="\f"} NR==<n>' file`. Grep several spellings (OCR of diacritics is noisy; Persian OCR is rough — try short substrings). Full titles, page offsets and what a cited number means: data/verification/sources/refs_online.json.

ARY (Aryanpur) is alphabetical by Persian headword; grep the Persian word in ARY_pages.txt or the Latin-caps transliteration in ARY_latin_index_pages.txt, note the [pdf page N] tag, and quote from that page (printed page = pdf page + 1).

189:Most interesting are the cases where from two or more traditions (usually including Homer and the Rig-Veda) it is possible to reconstruct a poetic phrase or formula con- sisting of two members. Such are the expres- sions ‘“‘imperishable fame,” *klewos ndhg’hitom (kleu-', dhg“hei-); “holy (men- tal) force,” *isorom menos (eis-', men-'); and the “weaver (or crafter) of words,” the Indo- European poet himself, *wek”om teks-on (wek”, teks-). The immortality of the gods (*n-mrto-, from mer-?) is emphasized anew by the vivid verb phrase nek-' tera-?, “to overcome death,” appearing in the Greek word nektar, the drink of the gods. And at least one three-member formula (in the sense of the word in traditional oral poetry) can be reconstructed for the poetic language of prayer, on the combined evidence of four languages, Latin, Umbrian, Avestan, and Sanskrit: “Protect, keep safe, man and cat- tle!” (pa- wi-ro- peku).
638:kleu-1, To hear. I. Extended form *kleus- in Germanic *hleuza- in Old English hléor, cheek (< “side of the face” < “ear”): LEER. II. Zero-grade form *klu-. 1. Germanic *hlustjan in Old English Alystan, to listen: LIsT*. 2. Ger- manic *hlusin6én in Old English Alysnan, to listen: LIs- TEN. 3. Suffixed lengthened form *kli-to- in Germanic *hlidaz, “heard,” loud, in: a. Old English Alid, loud: Loup; b. Old High German Aldti, sound: ABLAUT, UM- LauT. III. Suffixed form *klew-yo- in Greek kleiein, to praise, tell: Cio. [Pok. 1. Rleu- 605.]
639:kleu-2. To wash, clean. 1. Latin clodca, sewer, canal: CLOACA. 2. Zero-grade form *klu- in Greek kluzein, to wash out: CLYSTER; CATACLYSM. [Pok. 2. kleu- 607.] kleu-3. Possibly hook, peg. I. Extended zero-grade form *klud- possibly in Germanic *Aluta-, lot, portion (seman- tic development obscure). 1. Old English Alot, lot: Lor. 2. Dutch lot, lot: LOTTERY. 3. Old French lot (> French lot), lot, portion: LOTTO; ALLOT. II. Suffixed variant form *klau-do- in Latin claudere, to close (< “to lock with a hook, bolt”): CLAUSE, CLOISONNE, CLOISTER, CLOSE, (CLOSURE), (CLOZE); CONCLUDE, ECLOSION, EXCLUDE, INCLUDE, OCCLUDE, PRECLUDE, RECLUSE, SECLUDE. III. Variant form *k/dw-. 1. Suffixed form *kldw-i- in Latin cldvis, key: CEMBALO, CLAVICLE, CLAVIER, CLEF, KEVEL; CLAVICHORD, CONCLAVE, ENCLAVE. 2. Suffixed form *kldw-o- in: a. Latin cldévus, nail: CLOVE!, CLOY; b. Latin clava, club: CLAVATE; CLAVICORN, CLAVIFORM. 3. Suffixed form *k/dw-yo- in: a. Greek kleiein, to close: CLATHRATE; b. Greek verbal adjective kleistos, closed: CLEISTOGAMOUS, CLEISTOTHECIUM. [Pok. k/éu- 604.] klewo-. Bald. Variant *kal(a)wo- in Latin calvus, bald: CALVARIUM. [Pok. k,/ouo- 554.]

189:Most interesting are the cases where from two or more traditions (usually including Homer and the Rig-Veda) it is possible to reconstruct a poetic phrase or formula con- sisting of two members. Such are the expres- sions ‘“‘imperishable fame,” *klewos ndhg’hitom (kleu-', dhg“hei-); “holy (men- tal) force,” *isorom menos (eis-', men-'); and the “weaver (or crafter) of words,” the Indo- European poet himself, *wek”om teks-on (wek”, teks-). The immortality of the gods (*n-mrto-, from mer-?) is emphasized anew by the vivid verb phrase nek-' tera-?, “to overcome death,” appearing in the Greek word nektar, the drink of the gods. And at least one three-member formula (in the sense of the word in traditional oral poetry) can be reconstructed for the poetic language of prayer, on the combined evidence of four languages, Latin, Umbrian, Avestan, and Sanskrit: “Protect, keep safe, man and cat- tle!” (pa- wi-ro- peku).

Germanic *hlustjan in Old English Alystan, to listen: LIsT*. 2. Ger- manic *hlusin6én in Old English Alysnan, to listen: LIs- TEN. 3. Suffixed lengthened form *kli-to- in Germanic *hlidaz, “heard,” loud, in: a. Old English Alid, loud: Loup; b. Old High German Aldti, sound: ABLAUT, UM- LauT. III. Suffixed form *klew-yo- in Greek kleiein, to praise, tell: Cio. [Pok. 1. Rleu- 605.]
639:kleu-2. To wash, clean. 1. Latin clodca, sewer, canal: CLOACA. 2. Zero-grade form *klu- in Greek kluzein, to wash out: CLYSTER; CATACLYSM. [Pok. 2. kleu- 607.] kleu-3. Possibly hook, peg. I. Extended zero-grade form *klud- possibly in Germanic *Aluta-, lot, portion (seman- tic development obscure). 1. Old English Alot, lot: Lor. 2. Dutch lot, lot: LOTTERY. 3. Old French lot (> French lot), lot, portion: LOTTO; ALLOT. II. Suffixed variant form *klau-do- in Latin claudere, to close (< “to lock with a hook, bolt”): CLAUSE, CLOISONNE, CLOISTER, CLOSE, (CLOSURE), (CLOZE); CONCLUDE, ECLOSION, EXCLUDE, INCLUDE, OCCLUDE, PRECLUDE, RECLUSE, SECLUDE. You are helping verify etymologies from Ali Nourai's "An Etymological Dictionary of Persian, English and other Indo-European Languages" (1999), page 240 (PDF 270), root "Kleu 1" = PIE *ḱleu- "to hear" (Pokorny 605).

Research the IRANIAN branch on the web (Wiktionary en.wiktionary.org, Etymonline, Encyclopaedia Iranica iranicaonline.org, Wikipedia) and report findings. The chart claims:

- ROOT [Indo-European] Kleu 1 "to hear" (POK:605)
- #1 [Avestan] "sru 2, srav, xšnu, xšnaw" : to hear  ← from root
- #2 [Pahlavi] "ašnŭdan" : to hear  ← from #1
- #3 [Persian] šenīdan «شنیدن» : to hear (also شنودن، شنو، حرف شنو) ← from #2
- #4 [Avestan] "sravah : word, speech ; srū-ta : speech ; sraw : to read ; srâw : to sing" ← from root
- #5 [Persian] sarvâ «سروا (سرواد، سرواده)» : poem, story (also سرود، سرودن، سراییدن، سرای ۲) ← from #4
- #6 [Avestan] "hu-srav : well famed, famous ; dâuš-sravah : ill-famed" ← from root
- #7 [Pahlavi] "hu-srov" : well-famed, title of kings and in-laws ← from #6
- #8 [Persian] xosrow «خسرو (کسرىٰ)» : (well famed) king ; xosor «خُسُر (خسور، خسوره)» : father-in-law ; xošū «خُشو» : mother-in-law ← from #7
- #9 [Pahlavi] "du-srav" : ill famed, infamous ← from #6
- #11 [Avestan] "sraothra, sraosha" : ear, one who listens and follows ← from root
- #12 [Pahlavi] "srôsh" : one who obeys (God) ← from #11
- #13 [Persian] sorūsh «سروش» : one of God's angels ← from #12

KEY QUESTIONS to settle with sources:
1. Is NP شنیدن šenīdan really from Av. sru- via a form with xšnu/xšnaw? Note Nourai lumps Av. sru- "hear" with xšnu- "know/be satisfied". Modern view: MP ašnūdan/ašnaw- and NP شنیدن — Cheung (Etymological Dictionary of the Iranian Verb) derives it from Proto-Iranian *sru- (with prothetic vowel and a x-/ initial?), or from *xšnu-? What do Wiktionary/Cheung/Hasandust say? Which is right — is the initial š- from *sr- or from *xšn-?
2. سرود / سرودن / سراییدن / سروا — from Av. sraoθra / srav- ? What does Wiktionary say for سرود and سرودن and سراییدن?
3. خسرو Xosrow ← MP Husraw ← Av. Haosravah- / hu-sravah- "of good fame". Confirm.
4. Crucially: are خسر (xosor, father-in-law) and خشو (xošū, mother-in-law) really from hu-srav "well-famed"?? Modern scholarship derives them from PIE *sweḱuros / *sweḱrūs "father-in-law/mother-in-law" (Latin socer/socrus, Greek hekyros, Skt śvaśura-, Av. x˅asura-), i.e. from *swe- family words, NOT from *ḱleu-. Check Wiktionary for خسر / خسو / خشو and Proto-Iranian *hwasura-, and Pokorny *swekuro-. This is likely a DISPUTED node.
5. سروش Sorūš ← MP srōš ← Av. sraoša- "obedience, hearkening", the yazata Sraosha. Confirm; Av. sraoθra- "ear/hearing"?
6. Av. dāuš-sravah- "ill-famed" and MP dušraw / dušrav — confirm existence.

For EVERY web page you actually read, archive it by running:
python3 /home/sfmqrb/git/rishe/tools/fetch_source.py '<URL>' --note 'page 270, root Kleu 1, <what you used it for>'
(batch several in one Bash call). Only report URLs you actually fetched AND archived.

Report back: for each numbered claim, a verdict (confirmed / plausible / disputed) with the concrete forms and sound changes, plus the archived URLs. Be concrete about intermediate forms (Proto-Iranian, Avestan, Middle Persian per MacKenzie, New Persian). Do NOT write any report files; reply in your final message.

A. the 3d king of the Kayanian dynasty, mostly known as Kai-Xösröi [kdhwslwd, -Iwd'] 7133. 1138-17; with the patron. Siydvaxsan 116’; eschatological hero 887°. 99—100 passim. 1065; — ~ i Kavätän, founder of five cities 114? sqq., is probably the old Kayanian king of the heroic saga. — B. the Sassanid kings from Bahram I (273— 276) onwards assumed the title ka? (g.v.) and regarded themselves as Kayanians: Kai-Kavät (488—531), his son im bag Xösröi šāhān šah i Kavätän (531-579) 10921, known as anösak-ruvän 118%; on Baxt-— v. this w. — Gr Xoopöns, NP Xusrav; Av. (1738) žhaosravah-. The spell- ings are: 1. on coins: hwslwd, hwslwdy (already Prth); hwslwy (predominant un- der Khosroes II 590-628); once hwslw? and once hwslwty (!) v. Paruck 380- 384. 386-390; Hansen, Catrang 18-19; — 2. in the inseriptions: KZSPrth hwsrw, Gr. v. Xootew, Prs hwslwb,  which is also the spelling in three of the cities mention- ed 1141? sqq., certainly to be pronounced Xūsrūv = Arm Xosrov (but Syr Kösrö). In my opinion the BP form hwslwb' re- presents in reality hwslwdy, -b- being, as often at the end of the w., the cursive form of the letter d as written in the Ps.

=== NYB husrav
hu-ram [hwlm] cheerful, glad 67%; bliss- ful, of Paradise, comp. ~-tar 66’. — Paz. cüram; NP xurram; in some way or other to be connected with Av. (1511) ram- ‘to rest, to repose’. Cf the next w. and huraméh.
hu-rām [hwl’m] blissful, of Paradise 76}. 857-12, — Paz. hüräm, Skr v. šubhānanda ; < hu + rām < Av. (1524) räman- ‘rest, peace’, from the same root as the pre- ceding w.; cf rāmēnītār, rämisn; cf also NP ram.
hu-ramak [hwlmk'] having good herds of cattle 5076, with the gl. ku ramak 4 apdrik veh dānēt dästan ‘that is: it knows how to breed other cattle [than sheep, ete.] in the best way’. — V. ramak. Paz. hurama; translates Av. (1857) hvq0wa-.
huramēh abstr. of hu-ram (g.v.): ~ kartan to enjoy oneself 4?5.
hu-rät [hwlt'] of good munificence, mu- nificent 511, with the gl. ku rdteh veh dānēt kartan ‘that is: it knows how to practise munificence in the best way’. — V. rātēh.
hu-srav [hwslwb'] of good honour, re- nown; renowned, illustrious: comp. ~-tar
www .parsianjoman.org | col ak,
hu-srav
699. — OIr *hu-sravah-, Skr su-éravas-; Paz. zusrūb; MPrs adj. hwsrwg < *hu- srava-ka- (A-H II), v. srav and Xosrod.
husravéh abstr. of the preceding w.: renown 891. — Paz. xusrübi.
Hušētar [hwšytl] the first of the three still unborn sons of Zartuxšt who will appear in the trimillenial apocalyptic period: 7114. 9619.17.39. — Paz. Hušečar; from Av.  (384) Uxsyat.orata-.
Hušētarmāh [hwšytlm”h] the second ap- ocalyptic son of Zartuxšt who will appear after Hušētar: 7114, 988-14.16, 999. 11017. — Paz. Huseöarmäh; from Av. (384) Uz- šyat.nomah-, cf the spelling ?wšytnms DkM 44! (-ms inverse spelling of -mah).
hušk [hwšk'] dry, withered 197. 4124, — Av. (1840) huska- = OP; MPrthPrs hwék; NP zusk, cf hošitan. — 12814 hwsky: read hösak, q. v.
hu-tarist [hwtlst'] beautiful all round 5771, v. s. v. hu-örön and turist.
hu-taštak [hwt&tk'] well moulded, pl. cas. obl. ~-dn well moulded, beautifully shaped bowls 6014. — Av. (1823) hutästa- from taš-, v. tasitan.
hu-tohmčh [hwtwhrayh] good parentage 3917, — Abstr. of hu-tohm ‘of good seed’, v. tohm.

3446:"snavišneh [snwšnyh] 40? uncertain: Pourušasp went down to the waters of the Daiti river pat meno? kāmakēh (g.v., with a gl, v.s. v. apäyistan) u (pat) menči "snavišneh with the gl. ku ménoyan hamé sit. As the gl. is intended to explain snavišneh the very common w. sit ‘use, advantage' is little appropriate; most probably it should be emended do *snūt. For a vb. *snütan *snav-, however, no other support can be found, at least for the present, than the isolated hapaxlego- menon snus, n. sg. of snut. FrO XII, with the Phl gl. sökenet ‘he does useful work, serves'. Bthl (1630) regards this as a parallel form of (559) xšnu- (xšnav-) adj. ‘satisfying’, subst. ‘fulfilment of one’s duty’ from (557 sqq.) xšnav- ‘to satisfy’ and ‘to be satisfied’, and translates it ‘giving (another) what belongs to him by right, satisfying (another)’; he thinks the n. pr. Snaoya- (Yt. 13?9) belongs to this root (1627). Thus *snūtan snav- (most probably a NW vb.) possibly ‘to fulfill one’s (religious) duty’ : ‘in fulfilment of his duty towards Heaven’ with the explanation ‘he fulfilled his duty to- wards the heavenly beings’ (??).
3570:sūtē-karēh [swtyklyhy] supplication, en- treaty 1284, — sūtē- probably < OP *euti- from Av. (1648) srūtt-, v.s. v. srūtan and cf srav and sobdr.

Etymonline's `*kleu-` entry gives the standard cognate set: "Sanskrit *srnoti* 'hears,' *srutah* 'heard of, celebrated;' Greek *klyo* 'hear,' *klytos*…, *kleos* 'report, rumor, fame glory;' Latin *cluere*…; Old Church Slavonic *slusati* 'to hear,' *slava* 'fame, glory,' *slovo* 'word'."

Cognate with Sanskrit श्रवस् (śravas)." Semantic field: `*slava`, `*sluti`, `*slyšati`, `*slušati`, `*slȗxъ`. (Greek *kleos* and Av. *sravah-* belong to the same s-stem — not stated on that page but standard.)
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Slavic/slovo)

**#14b — *Slověninŭ* "Slav" ← *slovo* — DISPUTED; this is Nourai's weakest link.** Wiktionary's *main* etymology is the hydronym one: "With `*-ěninъ` ('-ian, inhabitant of') suffixed to the root of `*Slovǫta` ('the Dnieper') or another, similar river name; compare Russian Слуя (Sluja), Polish Sława, Sławica, Serbo-Croatian Slavnica. **The suffix *-ěninъ/*-janinъ is added only to geographical/territorial terms and place names, making it hard to assume other etymologies.** Further etymology unclear." Compare Lithuanian village Šlavė́nai on the river Šlavė̃. Derivation "From `*slovo` ('word; speech'), literally 'man of own speech, man who speaks the same language'" is filed under the heading **"Obsolete and alternative etymologies"**, alongside `*sluti`, `*slava`, Gołąb's `*swebʰen` (which invokes `*slovo` only as later *folk-etymological* influence), Masing/Stender-Petersen's Gothic loan, and Mikkola's `*leh₂wos`.

Etymonline is softer and still allows it: "from a shortening of Proto-Slavic *sloveninu 'a Slav,' which is **probably related to** *slovo 'word, speech,' which suggests the name originally identified a member of a speech community." It adds: "Max Vasmer, the authority for Slavic etymologies, **rejects** a connection to *slava 'glory, fame,' which, however, influenced Slav via **folk etymology**." So Vasmer's explicit rejection targets *slava*, not *slovo*; Wiktionary demotes *slovo* too on morphological grounds. Verdict: **plausible-but-disputed, and no longer the mainstream analysis.**
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Slavic/slověninъ ; https://www.etymonline.com/word/Slav)

**#15 — "Middle Greek *slabnovus*" — form is GARBLED; the chain itself is confirmed.** Correct Byzantine Greek: **Σκλαβηνός (Sklabēnós)** / Σθλαβηνός, pl. Σκλαβηνοί (6th c.), whence shortened **Σκλάβος (Sklábos)**, dated by etymonline to **c. 580**. Wiktionary Σκλάβος: "From earlier *Σκλαβηνός (Sklabēnós), *Σθλαβηνός (Sthlabēnós), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *slověninъ." Nourai's *slabnovus* is a mangling of *Sklabēnós* (and it carries a Latin -us ending it should not have). His gloss "Slav, also slaves taken from the Slavs" is right in substance. Note also the *reverse* hypothesis Wiktionary records and rejects (Σκλαβηνός ← σκῡλάω/σκῡλεύω "to strip a slain enemy") as "highly irregular derivation within Greek… contradicts the historical chronology."
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Σκλάβος)

**#16 — "Middle Latin *slavous*" — GARBLED; should be Late Latin *Sclavus* / Medieval Latin *sclavus*.** Etymonline dates Medieval Latin **Sclavus to c. 800**. Wiktionary: Medieval Latin *sclavus* "slave" "From Late Latin *Sclavus* ('Slav'), from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), from Proto-Slavic *slověninъ, because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages." The capital/lowercase split (Sclavus "Slav" vs sclavus "slave") is exactly Nourai's double gloss, so the semantics are right; only the spelling *slavous* is wrong (Latin *Slavus* without -c- is a later, humanist-era spelling).
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sclavus)

**#17/#19 — French → English "slave" — confirmed.** English *slave* c.1300 ← Middle English *sclave* ← Old French **esclave** (Old French also *Sclave*, Middle French *sclave*) ← Medieval Latin *sclavus*. Cognate outcomes: Italian *schiavo*, Spanish *esclavo*, German *Sklave*, Dutch *slaaf*. English *Slav* is attested **late 14c. as *Sclave***; "The reduction of scl- to sl- is regular in English (compare *slate*)… The spelling *Slav* is by 1866." The capital/lowercase split (Sclavus "Slav" vs sclavus "slave") is exactly Nourai's double gloss, so the semantics are right; only the spelling *slavous* is wrong (Latin *Slavus* without -c- is a later, humanist-era spelling).
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sclavus)

**#17/#19 — French → English "slave" — confirmed.** English *slave* c.1300 ← Middle English *sclave* ← Old French **esclave** (Old French also *Sclave*, Middle French *sclave*) ← Medieval Latin *sclavus*. Cognate outcomes: Italian *schiavo*, Spanish *esclavo*, German *Sklave*, Dutch *slaaf*. English *Slav* is attested **late 14c. as *Sclave***; "The reduction of scl- to sl- is regular in English (compare *slate*)… The spelling *Slav* is by 1866." So English has *two* borrowings of the same word (ethnonym and status-term), which the chart correctly splits.
(https://www.etymonline.com/word/slave ; https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/slave ; https://www.etymonline.com/word/Slav)

**#18 — Persian اسلاو / یوگوسلاوی / چکوسلواکی via French — UNVERIFIED (no source found either way).** Wiktionary's Persian entry اسلاو (eslâv) gives pronunciations only and **no etymology section at all**; fa.wiktionary یوگوسلاوی is a 2013 stub with no etymology; fa.wikipedia چکسلواکی cites only Czech *Československo* and English *Czechoslovakia*, not French. The only support for Nourai's French routing is indirect and phonetic: the Persian shapes چکسلواکی /čekoslovâki/ and یوگسلاوی /yugoslâvi/ match French *Tchécoslovaquie* / *Yougoslavie* (final -ie → -ی) rather than English *Czechoslovakia* / *Yugoslavia* (which would give -یا), and French was the dominant Western source for Persian neologisms in the Qajar/Pahlavi period. Treat as **plausible, unsourced**.
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/اسلاو ; https://fa.wiktionary.org/wiki/یوگوسلاوی ; https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/چکسلواکی)

**#20/#21 — Germanic *hlusinôn* "listen", *hlūdaz* "loud" → English listen, loud — confirmed, with one form correction.**
- *loud*: Wiktionary PGmc **`*hlūdaz`** "loud; famous" ← PIE `*ḱlutós` ← `*ḱlew-` ("The origin of the long vowel is unclear"); → OE *hlūd*, OHG *lūt*, OFris/OS *hlūd*. Etymonline agrees: OE *hlud*, PGmc `*hludaz` "heard", PIE `*klutos-`, cognates Skt *srutah*, Gk *klytos*, Lat *inclutus*. **Nourai's *hlūdaz* is exactly right.**
- *listen*: etymonline gives OE *hlysnan* (Mercian) / *lysna* (Northumbrian) from Proto-Germanic **`*hlusinon`** — Nourai's form matches etymonline/AHD verbatim. Wiktionary's OE entry instead reconstructs **`*hlusnijaną`**. Both trace to `*ḱlew-`; the discrepancy is a reconstruction-variant, not an error on Nourai's part. Note the modern *-t-* is secondary (influence of *list* v.2, cf. *glisten*).
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Germanic/hlūdaz ; https://www.etymonline.com/word/loud ; https://www.etymonline.com/word/listen ; https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hlysnan)

**#22 — Latin *cluere* "to be named" ← root — confirmed (with a lemma caveat).** Wiktionary lemmatizes **clueō** (2nd-conj., defective — no passive, perfect or supine) "to be called or named; to be reputed", "From Proto-Italic *kluēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- ('to hear')", cognates Lith. *klausýti*, OCS *slušati*, Skt *śroṣati*, Gk *kléos*. *cluō/cluere* is listed as an alternative form of *clueō*. **Caveat:** there is a *homonymous* Latin `cluō` "to purge/clean" (syn. *pūrgō*) from PIE `*ḱlewH-`, with cognates Goth. *hlūtrs*, Welsh *clir*, Gk *klúdōn*, and derivative *cloāca* — a different root, not to be confused with Nourai's node.
(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/clueo ; https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/cluo)

**#23 — English "client" ← *cluere* — DISPUTED, and Nourai's AHD citation is misattributed.** Two competing derivations:
- **Watkins/AHD and etymonline put *client* under `*klei-` "to lean", not `*kleu-`.** Etymonline's *client*: "Latin *clientem* (nominative *cliens*) 'follower, retainer'… related to *clinare* 'to incline, bend,' from PIE root `*klei-` 'to lean'" — "one who leans on another for protection." Etymonline's `*klei-` word list explicitly contains **client** (alongside climate, clinic, decline, incline, lean, ladder, lid…), while its `*kleu-` list — *listen, loud, leer, list, Slav, slave, Slavic, Slovene, Yugoslav*, Cleon, Clio, Pericles… — **does not contain client**. Since Nourai cites "AHD" for this node, the citation does not support the claim as drawn.
- **However, the *cluere* derivation is not fringe.** Wiktionary *cliens* gives it as the **first** option: "Possibly an alteration of *cluēns*, present active participle of *clueō* ('to be called, named, esteemed'). **Alternatively** from *clīnō* ('to lean'). In this case ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- ('to incline')." Wiktionary's *clueō* entry likewise lists "cluēns/cliēns" among its descendants ("source of English *client*"). This is the older 19th-c. view (cliens = "the one who is named/called on / who has a name from his patron") that Wiktionary still carries.

**Verdict: disputed rather than flatly wrong** — Nourai has picked the minority side, but he attributes it to AHD, which holds the opposite. Flag the reference, not just the arrow.
(https://www.etymonline.com/word/client ; https://www.etymonline.com/word/*klei- ; https://www.etymonline.com/word/*kleu- ; https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/cliens)

## Summary of corrections to the chart
1. `slabnovus` (#15) → **Σκλαβηνός (Sklabēnós)**, Byz. Gk., 6th c.; short form **Σκλάβος (Sklábos)** c. 580.
2. `slavous` (#16) → **Sclavus** (Late Latin, "Slav", c. 800) / **sclavus** (Medieval Latin, "slave").
3. #14 *Slověninŭ* ← *slovo*: mark **disputed** — Wiktionary files it under obsolete etymologies and prefers a river-name base (`*Slovǫta`), on the grounds that `*-ěninъ` attaches only to place names; Vasmer separately rejects the *slava* link as folk etymology.
4. #23 *client* ← *cluere*: mark **disputed / reference wrong** — AHD and etymonline put *client* under `*klei-` "to lean" (< *clinare*); only Wiktionary preserves the *cluēns* alternative.
5. Minor: #22's lemma is properly **clueō** (*cluere* is the alt-form infinitive), and must be kept distinct from homonymous *cluō* "to purge" < `*ḱlewH-`.
6. #20's `hlusinôn` matches etymonline/AHD; Wiktionary's competing reconstruction is `*hlusnijaną`. `hlūdaz` is correct as printed.</result>

Berneker 162f. Walde-P. 1.369.
26181:15.41 HEAR
26222:ey : 1036 15.41-15.44. The verbs for ‘hear’, de- noting the actual perception, may also be used for ‘listen’, especially in the im- perative. But generally there are also distinctive words for ‘listen’. Most of these are cognate with the words for ‘hear’, either those so used in the same language (NHG horchen : héren, NE harken : hear, Russ. slugat’ : sly- Sat’) or in other languages (NE listen, etc. : Grk. xAtw, etc.). In a Celtic group ‘listen’ rests on the notion of ‘be silent, be still’, which elsewhere is a sec- ondary association of ‘listen’ (cf. below, 4). Other secondary developments of ‘listen’ are ‘listen for’ > ‘watch for, wait for’ (OF hlosnian) and ‘be atten- tive to’, esp. ‘obey’ (Lat. auscultare, NHG gehorchen, Dan. lyde, Sw. lyda, Lith. klausyti, ChSl. poslusati, etc.).

Nourai's own FFD:64 (Abolghasemi) reconstructs \*šnav/\*šnu, and his BQT:1304 (Mo'in) derives it from OP āxšnavamiy; Hübschmann p.82 says a root xšnū "sich nicht mit zd. sru vereinigen lassen würde". Only Horn 177 backs Nourai.
- **#8 Persian xosrow / xosor / xošū** — the chart's worst error. خسرو is right (< MP Husraw < \*hu-sravah-), but خسر/خسور "father-in-law" and خشو "mother-in-law" are from PIE \*sweḱuros / \*sweḱruh₂ (Av. x°asura-, Skt śvaśura-/śvaśrū-, Lat. socer/socrus). Horn no. 486-487 — on p.108, the very page Nourai cites — says so, as do Hübschmann p.213 and Mo'in's own footnote on BQT p.749. The trap is the homonymy of older NP xusrū "mother-in-law" with خسرو "king", which the Borhan merged in one article.
- **#14 Old Slavic Slověninŭ ← slovo** — Klein 1456 is quoted correctly, but Wiktionary/Slavistics now files this under "obsolete etymologies" and prefers a river-name base (\*Slovǫta), since \*-ěninъ attaches only to place names.
- **#23 English client ← cluere** — Watkins/AHD (the reference Nourai cites) puts CLIENT under \*klei- "lean"; Klein s.v. client: "The usual derivation of L. cliens from the stem of cluere ... is erroneous."
